newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico wins breakthough in U.S. death row case.
newsitem.headline: Mexico wins breakthough in U.S. death row case.

text.p: Mexico on Thursday said there was a glimmer of hope for a Mexican citizen condemned to death next week in a Texas jail after the U.S. State Department agreed to intervene.

The Mexican Foreign Ministry has pressed Washington to step in, telling the State Department via diplomatic notes that the condemned man, Irnineo Tristan Montoya, was never informed when he was arrested of his right to contact Mexican consular officials.
That right, it said, is enshrined in the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations and may have been violated by police in Brownsville, Texas, when Tristan was arrested in 1986.

In a statement, the ministry said the State Department on Thursday had ordered Texas Gov. George Bush to launch an investigation into the matter and had urged him to inform Washington of its findings before Tristan is executed.
If it turns out the convention was violated, the State Department told Bush that should be weighed in deciding whether Tristan had been given a fair trial.
"That in no way means that the death sentance will not be carried out. But it does represent a new possibility of avoiding the fatal outcome," the Foreign Ministry said.
The case of Tristan, who faces death by lethal injection on June 18, has begun to whip up passions in Mexico, where the death penalty is outlawed and considered "cruel and inhuman" by the government.

Tristan is on death row in a Texas jail, convicted of murder and rape. Two months ago another Mexican was released after 14 years on death row. He has since returned to Mexico and starred in a television soap opera.
